title: Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs (With Examples)
seoTitle: Fixed vs Variable Costs: Examples & Formulas
description: Compare fixed and variable costs in total and per unit. Classify mixed expenses, calculate total fixed cost, and check service, restaurant and product examples.
metaDescription: Compare fixed vs variable costs with examples, total fixed cost and variable cost per unit formulas, mixed-cost checks, charts and worked break-even scenarios.

opening: Learn fixed costs vs variable costs examples with clear formulas, realistic scenarios, and steps to calculate contribution margin and break-even sales.
features: Assumptions and cost behavior made visible
html:
Fixed costs stay the same in total over a relevant level of activity, while variable costs rise or fall with the number of products or services you sell. For pricing and break-even planning, you need to separate the two because fixed costs are spread across sales, but variable costs are attached to each sale.

Quick answer: Fixed costs do not change in total when sales volume changes, such as rent or a software subscription. Variable costs change with each unit sold, such as ingredients, packaging, or sales commissions. Add fixed costs to find your operating base; subtract variable cost per sale from price to see what each sale contributes toward profit.

Fixed vs variable costs: compare total cost and cost per unit

Cost behavior within one stated period and relevant activity range
QuestionFixed costVariable cost
What happens to the total?Unchanged within the stated rangeChanges with the matching activity driver
What happens per unit?Falls as the same commitment is spread over more unitsConstant only under a linear per-unit assumption
At zero activity?The commitment can remain payableZero for a purely volume-driven cost; check minimum commitments
Typical conditional examplesA monthly premises lease or guaranteed salaryMaterial consumed, per-order packaging or a sales commission

Choose the driver before assigning a label: units produced, jobs completed, miles driven and sales dollars are different measures. A percentage card fee varies with collected revenue, so a discount can change its dollar cost per order. Fixed does not mean permanent, and variable does not mean discretionary. Both labels describe behavior over a defined time and range.

Total fixed cost formula and variable cost per unit

Reconciled formulas using the existing 80-visit fictional example, USD
MeasureFormulaWorked result
Total variable costVariable cost per visit × completed visits$81 × 80 = $6,480
Total costTotal fixed cost + total variable cost$3,200 + $6,480 = $9,680
Total fixed costTotal cost − total variable cost$9,680 − $6,480 = $3,200
Variable cost per unitTotal variable cost ÷ matching units$6,480 ÷ 80 = $81 per visit
Fixed cost per unitTotal fixed cost ÷ matching units$3,200 ÷ 80 = $40 per visit
Average total cost per unitTotal cost ÷ matching units$9,680 ÷ 80 = $121 per visit

The subtraction formula works only when total cost and variable cost cover the same costs, activity and period. It does not identify cost behavior from one unexplained bill. For total fixed cost = total cost − (variable cost per unit × units), independently establish the per-unit rate first. At zero units, total fixed cost can still be measured, but per-unit divisions are undefined.

To estimate a mixed bill from activity records, use the high-low method and its outlier checks. For the next calculation, follow the contribution-margin method and break-even formulas for units and sales dollars. Keep this page as the cost-classification reference rather than treating all four methods as interchangeable.

The direct answer

A fixed cost remains constant in total for a period, provided you stay within a normal operating range. If your shop sells 100 or 200 items this month, its monthly rent may still be $2,000. Other examples can include a basic insurance premium, a salaried office manager, accounting software, and a business license fee.

A variable cost changes in total as activity changes. If you make twice as many products, you generally buy more materials. If you serve more customers, you may use more ingredients, disposable supplies, shipping materials, or transaction-based labor. A cost that is $4 per unit creates $400 of total cost at 100 units and $800 at 200 units.

Use this basic structure:

  • Total fixed costs: costs that do not change in total with short-term volume.
  • Variable cost per unit: the cost directly associated with one unit, order, job, or customer.
  • Contribution margin per unit: selling price minus variable cost per unit.
  • Operating profit: total sales minus total variable costs minus total fixed costs.

For example, if you charge $30 for a service and spend $12 on supplies and payment-related costs, your contribution margin is $18 per service. If monthly fixed costs are $1,800, you need 100 services to cover that fixed-cost base because $1,800 ÷ $18 = 100. Sales above that point can contribute to operating profit, assuming the cost assumptions remain accurate.

What changes the answer

The time period matters. Rent is usually fixed month to month. Over several years, a lease may renew at a higher amount. State the time frame for your analysis.

The activity range matters. A small bakery may use its existing oven for 500 items a week. If demand reaches 1,000 items, it may need another oven or an extra shift. The original equipment cost behaves like a fixed cost within the first range, then the business takes a step up to a higher fixed-cost level.

Some costs are mixed. A phone plan can include a fixed monthly charge plus usage fees. A delivery arrangement can include a base fee plus a per-mile charge. Separate the base and usage portions when you can. If you cannot separate them precisely, make a reasonable estimate and label it as an assumption.

The unit must be clear. For a house cleaner, the unit might be one cleaning job. For a restaurant, it might be one meal, one order, or one cover. For a subscription business, a monthly subscriber may be the useful unit. Choose a unit that matches how you price and serve customers.

Timing is not the same as behavior. An annual insurance bill can create a large cash payment in one month, but the underlying expense may cover twelve months. Pricing policies can change variable cost. A discount may lower your revenue per unit without lowering ingredients, labor, or fulfillment costs. Free shipping may turn a cost you normally pass to the customer into a variable cost you absorb. Review the actual offer, not only the standard price.

Worked examples: Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs (With Examples)

Scenario 1: House cleaning service

You charge $160 for a standard cleaning. Supplies cost $10 per job, payment processing averages $5 per job, and you pay a cleaner $85 per completed job. The variable cost per job is therefore $100:

$10 + $5 + $85 = $100

The contribution margin is $60 per job:

$160 - $100 = $60

Your monthly fixed costs are $2,400. They include insurance, scheduling software, phone service, storage, and a regular administrative wage. The break-even volume is:

$2,400 ÷ $60 = 40 jobs

At 40 jobs, revenue is $6,400 and variable costs are $4,000. The remaining $2,400 covers fixed costs, so operating profit is $0. At 45 jobs, revenue is $7,200 and variable costs are $4,500. After fixed costs, operating profit is $300:

$7,200 - $4,500 - $2,400 = $300

That calculation also shows why a price increase should be tested against demand. An extra $10 per job would increase contribution margin if job volume and variable cost stayed the same, but the result changes if the higher price reduces bookings. For related pricing decisions, see margin and markup.

Scenario 2: Small restaurant menu item

A restaurant sells a bowl for $14. Ingredients cost $4.20, the disposable container costs $0.60 for takeout orders, and a per-order fee averages $0.40. For a takeout bowl, variable cost is $5.20:

$4.20 + $0.60 + $0.40 = $5.20

The contribution margin is $8.80:

$14.00 - $5.20 = $8.80

Suppose monthly fixed costs allocated to the restaurant operation are $17,600. This includes rent, core salaried labor, insurance, and recurring systems. The number of bowls needed to cover that amount, if the bowl were the only item analyzed, is 2,000:

$17,600 ÷ $8.80 = 2,000 bowls

At 2,300 bowls, sales are $32,200. Variable costs are $11,960, calculated as 2,300 × $5.20. Operating profit after the stated fixed costs is $2,640:

$32,200 - $11,960 - $17,600 = $2,640

ways to lower your break-even point for a related pricing framework.

Scenario 3: Handmade product sold online

You sell a candle for $28. Wax and fragrance cost $6.50, the jar and label cost $3.50, packaging costs $2, and average payment and marketplace fees are $2.80. Total variable cost is $14.80:

$6.50 + $3.50 + $2.00 + $2.80 = $14.80

Contribution margin is $13.20 per candle:

$28.00 - $14.80 = $13.20

Monthly fixed costs are $1,584 for design software, insurance, a small studio, and baseline marketing subscriptions. Break-even volume is 120 candles:

$1,584 ÷ $13.20 = 120 candles

If you sell 150 candles, revenue is $4,200 and variable cost is $2,220. Operating profit is $396 after fixed costs:

$4,200 - $2,220 - $1,584 = $396

Classify common expenses by the actual arrangement

Cost behavior is conditional; these are examples, not universal accounting rules
ExpenseWhat to check
Wages and direct laborA guaranteed salary may remain fixed; job-paid hours can vary. An additional shift can create a step cost.
Direct materials and shippingMaterials used and per-order carriage commonly vary; a shipping subscription or minimum commitment can add a fixed component.
Utilities and electricitySeparate the standing charge from usage charges; a capacity tariff or threshold can change the relationship.
DepreciationStraight-line depreciation is commonly a fixed period expense; units-of-production depreciation varies with usage. Depreciation is not the same as an equipment cash payment.
AdvertisingA committed campaign budget can be fixed for a period; a fee per conversion or completed sale can vary. Use the actual contract and attribution boundary.
Cost of goods soldCOGS is a functional classification and can contain fixed production overhead. It is not automatically identical to all variable expenses.

Variable cost per activity unit = the selected total variable cost ÷ its matching activity. For inspection work, divide by comparable inspections; for delivery, mileage may be the driver. A variable-cost diagram shows the selected pool rising with activity; a mixed-cost line starts above zero because it includes a fixed component. Rebuild the model outside its relevant range. Use flexible budgeting to separate changed activity from spending differences without scaling every cost as variable.

How to run your own numbers

Start with one period, such as one month, and one unit of activity. A job, order, meal, or product is usually easier to analyze than a vague “customer.” Write down the price you actually collect, after routine discounts, rather than the list price.

Use the MyBreakeven calculator to test your assumptions.

Next, list every cost that increases when you deliver one more unit. Include materials, packaging, per-order fees, shipping you pay, commissions, and labor that is paid per job or hour of production. Divide the total by expected units to estimate variable cost per unit. Keep a note beside each estimate so you can replace it with actual results later.

Then total the costs that remain for the period even if you sell nothing. Include recurring rent, baseline payroll, insurance, subscriptions, licenses, and planned overhead. Do not count the same cost in both lists.

Use these formulas:

Contribution margin per unit = selling price per unit - variable cost per unit

Break-even units = total fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit

Operating profit = (units sold × contribution margin per unit) - total fixed costs

How to calculate variable cost per unit from your own jobs

For a service business, begin with completed jobs from one consistent period. Imagine a cleaning team delivered 80 standard visits last month. Supplies consumed on those visits cost an illustrative $640, payment fees were $240, and labor paid specifically to complete the visits was $5,600. These costs total $6,480. Divide by the 80 completed visits: $6,480 ÷ 80 = $81 variable cost per visit. At a collected price of $145 per visit, each job contributes $145 − $81 = $64 before monthly fixed costs.

One month of standard visitsIllustrative totalPer completed visit
Supplies used$640$8
Per-payment fees$240$3
Paid job labor$5,600$70
Variable cost$6,480$81

Suppose the business also has $3,200 monthly fixed costs, including planned administration and owner pay not already counted as per-job labor. Break-even is $3,200 ÷ $64 = 50 completed standard visits. At 40 visits, contribution is $2,560 and the model is $640 short. At 60, contribution is $3,840 and the model leaves $640 after fixed costs. That holds only while the job mix, collected price, per-job cost and available staff remain close to the assumptions. These are fictional example numbers, not typical US cleaning prices.

If a phone plan has a $95 base charge plus $0.30 for each booking, put the $95 in the period's fixed costs and $0.30 in cost per booking. A full $119 bill for 80 bookings is not $119 of variable cost; allocating the fixed base to every booking and also entering $95 as fixed would count it twice. If you run out of crew capacity at 50 visits and must pay a new guaranteed shift, calculate a second range with that added fixed or step cost instead of projecting the original $64 contribution indefinitely. Our contribution margin guide shows how this per-job amount flows into sales goals.

Common mistakes

Calling every recurring cost fixed. A monthly bill may contain a usage component. Separate the base charge from the amount that grows with activity.

Ignoring labor that follows sales. If you pay someone per job, per item, or per hour worked, that labor belongs in the variable-cost calculation for the relevant decision. Otherwise, your contribution margin will look too high.

Using revenue instead of contribution margin. Revenue does not show what remains after fulfilling an order. Break-even volume based only on price will understate the sales needed.

Mixing cash timing with cost behavior. An annual renewal is not automatically a variable cost because cash leaves the bank once a year. Spread the expense for operating analysis while separately planning the cash payment.

Forgetting discounts, refunds, and waste. Your real selling price may be lower than the advertised price. Your real material usage may be higher than the recipe or bill of materials. Use observed averages when possible.

Rounding too early. Keep cents through the contribution-margin calculation. Round the final break-even unit target up because partial units do not cover a real sales target.

Separate average cost from variable cost and step costs

Average total cost per job changes when fixed costs are spread over a different number of jobs. In a separate illustration with $3,200 monthly fixed costs and $81 variable cost per job, 40 jobs cost $3,200 + 40 × $81 = $6,440, averaging $161 each. At 80 jobs, total cost is $9,680, averaging $121 each. Variable cost remains $81 within the assumed operating range.

Do not enter the $121 average as variable cost while also entering $3,200 fixed costs: that would count the fixed allocation twice. Nor should the declining average be used to promise that every additional job becomes cheaper.

Now suppose exceeding 60 jobs requires an extra $800 monthly commitment. At 70 jobs, fixed costs become $4,000 and total cost is $4,000 + 70 × $81 = $9,670. At a $145 price, revenue is $10,150 and the modeled surplus is $480. Ignoring the step would overstate that surplus by $800.

Write down the capacity threshold, commitment duration and which charges apply to existing as well as new jobs. A subscription upgrade that changes the fee on every order needs a whole-period recalculation, not just a fee applied to the extra orders.

Estimate mixed costs without double-counting

A fixed monthly vehicle commitment plus usage-dependent running costs is a mixed cost. If comparable observations show $1,640 at 80 equivalent visits and $2,440 at 280, the two-point estimate is ($2,440 − $1,640) ÷ (280 − 80) = $4 per visit; its monthly fixed component is $1,320. Select the high and low observations by activity, not cost, and inspect all intermediate records. The high-low method calculator and six-month example shows why a high repair bill can distort a model.

Cost behavior and traceability are different classifications: a cost can be directly attributable to a service while remaining fixed for the month, or indirect yet variable with activity. State the cost object and relevant range. After splitting a mixed cost, enter its fixed component once in overhead and variable component once per activity unit; do not add the original total again.

Fixed and variable cost curves: total cost versus cost per unit

Use the axes before interpreting a curve. In this independent fictional period, total fixed cost is $2,000, total variable cost is $20 × activity and a separate mixed-cost example is $1,000 + $10 × activity. The fixed line is horizontal on a total-cost chart; it is not horizontal on a cost-per-unit chart. These are three separate cost examples, not three components to add together.

Cost curves in numbers, fictional USD per period
ActivityFixed totalVariable totalMixed totalFixed per unit
02,00001,000Undefined
502,0001,0001,50040
1002,0002,0002,00020
2002,0004,0003,00010

At positive activity the variable cost per unit stays $20 under the assumption, while fixed cost per unit falls as the same $2,000 is spread across more units. At zero activity, a per-unit cost cannot be calculated. The mixed cost per unit falls from $30 at 50 units to $15 at 200, even though its total rises. A declining average therefore does not prove the total bill fell.

A capacity step can invalidate the old line

Suppose a separate staffing arrangement costs $2,000 through 100 jobs and requires a second $2,000 shift for 101–200 jobs. The fixed commitment is $2,000 at 100 jobs and $4,000 at 101. It is a step schedule, not the horizontal $2,000 assumption used in the chart. Review the contract and practical capacity; do not extend a line beyond its relevant range.

Accounting function is a separate dimension. An expense may be selling OPEX and variable, or administrative OPEX and fixed; production costs can also contain fixed and variable elements. The operating-expense guide owns classification against COGS, while the operating-margin calculator subtracts compatible statement totals. Do not transfer every OPEX line into a variable-cost field merely because it is an operating expense.

Compare a higher fixed commitment with a higher per-order charge

Consider two independent fictional fulfillment arrangements for identical service quality and scope. Option A costs $4,800 a month plus $20 per order; option B costs $1,200 plus $50 per order. They have equal modeled total cost at ($4,800 − $1,200) ÷ ($50 − $20) = 120 orders: each costs $7,200. At 80 orders A costs $6,400 and B $5,200; at 160 orders A costs $8,000 and B $9,200.

This is a cost-indifference point, not the business’s sales break-even point. It excludes selling price, financing, switching costs, capacity and contract minimums beyond those stated. Check those conditions before selecting an arrangement. The make-or-buy decision guide covers avoidable costs and capacity; the CVP guide shows how selling price and contribution change the profit calculation.

Method references and example boundaries

OpenStax’s managerial-accounting chapter explains total versus per-unit behavior and relevant ranges. Xero’s cost guide provides a business-oriented comparison; its UK-specific tax examples are not US accounting rules. This page’s calculations are independently constructed fictional examples. Loan principal payments are financing cash outflows, not automatically operating expenses: keep the payment calendar separate from the cost-behavior model. Check the working-capital balance and asset quality before assuming a profitable operating plan also has enough cash to pay those commitments.

Distinguish incremental tiers from an all-units price change

A lower rate above a threshold can mean two different contracts. In this fictional 0–200-order operating range, both arrangements have a $600 fixed monthly commitment. Contract A charges $8 for each of the first 100 orders, then $6 only for additional orders. Contract B charges $8 per order through 100; if qualifying monthly volume exceeds 100, its $6 rate applies to every order in that month. Assume identical scope and no other charges.

Original contract comparison; illustrative USD per month
OrdersA: incremental tiersB: all-units rateWhy they differ
80600 + 80 × 8 = 1,240600 + 80 × 8 = 1,240No threshold crossed
100600 + 100 × 8 = 1,400600 + 100 × 8 = 1,400Threshold not exceeded
101600 + 100 × 8 + 1 × 6 = 1,406600 + 101 × 6 = 1,206B reprices all qualifying orders
150600 + 100 × 8 + 50 × 6 = 1,700600 + 150 × 6 = 1,500A retains the first-tier charge

For contract A, total cost is 600 + 8 × MIN(Q,100) + 6 × MAX(Q − 100,0). For contract B it is 600 + IF(Q ≤ 100,8 × Q,6 × Q). These spreadsheet-style expressions require nonnegative whole Q within the stated range. The $600 remains fixed; the usage charge follows the applicable piecewise schedule.

At the 101st order, A’s total bill rises by $6. B’s modeled bill falls by $194 because the prior 100 orders also receive the $2 reduction: $6 for the extra order minus $200 of repricing. Do not generalize that result to a real supplier without verifying eligibility, minimum commitments, credits and the period when the rebate is earned. An annual purchasing rebate is not automatically available in a monthly cost model.

A single $6 or $8 rate cannot describe every point in both contracts. Nor is total bill divided by orders the variable rate: it includes the $600 fixed allocation. Keep the schedule, driver and activity range in the input record. For inventory, distinguish purchased units from consumed or sold units before assigning a period expense. The high-low estimation guide does not turn a known tier schedule into one reliable straight line; the transaction-fee allocation example shows the parallel need to define the selling unit.

OpenStax’s cost-behavior chapter explains why a relevant range and the activity driver matter. The two supplier arrangements here are original hypothetical cases, not claims about a named provider’s current prices.

faq.q: What is the variable cost per unit formula?
faq.a: Add the costs that increase when you deliver the units in a comparable period, then divide by the number of completed units. Check that each expense is included once and the units share a comparable scope.

faq.q: Is an hourly wage always a variable cost?
faq.a: Job-paid production time often changes with completed work, but a guaranteed shift may remain payable even if bookings fall. Model the actual pay arrangement and staffing range rather than assuming all labor behaves the same way.

faq.q: Can an annual payment be a fixed cost?
faq.a: Yes. Fixed and variable describe cost behavior as activity changes, not the date cash leaves the account. Plan the annual cash payment separately from the operating analysis.

faq.q: What if one job takes twice as long as another?
faq.a: Use job types or a weighted mix rather than one average across unlike services. A deep clean and a standard maintenance visit may need separate per-job labor and price assumptions.

faq.q: Are payment-processing fees fixed or variable?
faq.a: A per-transaction or percentage fee varies with the matching sales activity. A monthly account charge or minimum can add a fixed component. Separate the contract’s base and usage amounts without counting either twice.

faq.q: Can a cost be partly fixed and partly variable?
faq.a: Yes. A base subscription plus a per-order charge is a simple example. Enter the base in monthly commitments and the incremental charge in sale-dependent cost, each counted once.

faq.q: How do you calculate total fixed cost?
faq.a: Subtract total variable cost from total cost for the same period and scope. If the variable rate is independently known, total fixed cost equals total cost minus variable cost per unit multiplied by units. In this guide, $9,680 minus $81 times 80 visits equals $3,200.

faq.q: Does a lower tiered rate apply to all units or only extra units?
faq.a: The contract determines that. An incremental tier changes the charge only for units in that tier. An all-units arrangement can reprice every qualifying unit when a threshold is met. Record the applicable range and rebate timing before using either rate in a contribution calculation.
